Best Protein Bars Without Sugar Alcohols - Ranking 919+ Qualified Bars

We reviewed 1245 protein bars available in the US for sugar alcohols like Maltitol, Erythritol, Isomalto-oligosaccharides (IMO), Sorbitol, Xylitol, and Isomalt. It feels like sugar alcohols are everywhere, but the good news is that only about 26% of all protein bars have a sugar alcohol on their ingredient label. We break down and rank the best protein bars without sugar alcohols by category, brand, and macros. Not just us telling you the flavors we like.

What "no sugar alcohols" actually means

Sugar alcohols are the sweeteners bar makers reach for when they want a low sugar number on the label without giving up sweetness. This guide screens every bar for six of them: maltitol, erythritol, sorbitol, xylitol, isomalt, and isomalto-oligosaccharides (IMO), a prebiotic fiber syrup that behaves the same way on a label even though it isn't technically a sugar alcohol.

26% of the 1245 bars in our database still have a sugar alcohol on the label. Here is how often each one shows up, and where it usually hides.

Maltitol
202 bars16%
The most common sugar alcohol on the list, used for bulk and sweetness in low-sugar bars. Well known for causing GI distress at typical serving sizes.
Found in: 1st Phorm, 1st Tee, Alani, Anabar
and 26 moreHide, BSN, BalanceDiet, Barebells, Crave, David, Equate, FITCRUNCH, Fiber One, Fulfil, GNC Total Lean, Genius Gourmet, Ghost, JiMMYBAR!, Love Good, MRE BAR, MTN OPS, Met-RX, Misfits, Mucho, Musashi, NuGo, One, Pure Protein, SOAR, Wonderslim, think!
Erythritol
91 bars7%
A fermented sugar alcohol with a smaller GI-distress footprint than maltitol, usually paired with stevia or monk fruit in "clean" low-sugar formulas.
Found in: Atkins, Battle Bars, Genius Gourmet, JustNosh
and 17 moreHide, KetoBars.com, Legendary, Legion, Love Good, Mosh, Mucho, Musashi, MyProtein, Neoh, Nick's, No Cow, Orgain, Perfect Keto, Pure Protein, Quest, SOAR, think!
Isomalto-oligosaccharides (IMO)
52 bars4%
A prebiotic fiber syrup that also sweetens, common in bars marketing a low net-carb count. Scored here alongside true sugar alcohols since it behaves the same way on a label.
Found in: Anabar, BSN, BalanceDiet, Daryl's Bars
and 5 moreHide, One, Orgain, Raw Rev, Wonderslim, think!
Sorbitol
39 bars3%
A sugar alcohol with a strong laxative effect at moderate doses, most common in hard candy-style coatings and confectionery-style layers.
Found in: 1st Phorm, BalanceDiet, Built, FITCRUNCH
and 5 moreHide, GNC Total Lean, Gatorade, Ghost, MTN OPS, Neoh
Xylitol
8 bars1%
A sugar alcohol close to sucrose in sweetness, common in chocolate coatings; tolerated well by most people but a known GI trigger at higher doses.
Found in: Barebells, Nick's, form
Isomalt
8 bars1%
A low-glycemic bulk sweetener often used in chocolate-style coatings, similar mouthfeel to sugar with about half the calories.
Found in: BalanceDiet, Fiber One, MyProtein, UNiTE
and 1 moreHide, Wonderslim

If not sugar alcohols, then what?

Cutting sugar alcohols doesn't mean cutting sweetness. The 919 bars in this guide get their sweetness from two different places, and they show up very differently on the label.

Natural sugars, count fully toward the Sugars line

These are real sugar. They add grams to the Sugars and Added Sugars lines just like the sugar in a candy bar would, they just come from a whole-food or less processed source instead of a lab.

Dates
226 bars26%
A whole fruit, counts fully toward the Sugars line, but comes with fiber and micronutrients maltitol doesn’t.
Cane Sugar
236 bars27%
Straightforward table sugar. Counts as sugar and added sugar, no different from what’s in a candy bar.
Honey
200 bars23%
Counts fully as sugar on the label, same as cane sugar, just from a different source.
Brown Rice Syrup
107 bars12%
A glucose-heavy syrup used for texture and sweetness. Counts as sugar, higher glycemic impact than most alternatives here.
Agave
83 bars10%
Higher in fructose than table sugar. Still counts fully as sugar on the label.
Maple Syrup
51 bars6%
Counts as sugar, brings trace minerals table sugar doesn’t.

Zero-calorie alternatives, won't trigger this screen either

These sweeteners are not sugar alcohols and don't get counted as sugar. They're the closest thing to a free pass: sweetness with no calories, no grams on the Sugars line, and none of the digestive baggage sugar alcohols carry.

Monk Fruit
112 bars13%
Zero calories, zero grams of sugar. Sweetness comes from mogrosides, not a sugar molecule, so it doesn’t touch the sugar line or the sugar alcohol line.
Stevia
88 bars10%
Zero calories, zero sugar. Plant-derived, extracted from the stevia leaf rather than manufactured from a sugar molecule the way maltitol is.
Allulose
87 bars10%
A rare sugar that occurs naturally in small amounts in foods like figs. The FDA doesn’t require it to be counted as sugar or added sugar, and it’s not a sugar alcohol either.
Glycerin is a sugar alcohol gray area
  • Glycerin (glycerol) shows up in 339 of the 919 "no sugar alcohol" bars on this page (37%)
  • More than any single sugar alcohol we screen for
  • Glycerin is chemically a sugar alcohol, but we don't count it against a bar here

Here's why we don't include glycerin as a sugar alcohol

Glycerin (also listed as glycerol) is chemically a sugar alcohol and belongs to the same family as maltitol, erythritol, and xylitol. Using a chemistry definition, it belongs on this screen. (At least to the best of our understanding, as definitely NOT chemists.) However, we don't use it as a factor on our No Sugar Alcohols page. We'll do our best to show our work and explain why.

It's important to note that ingredients can serve more than one function. Maltitol is typically added as a sugar substitute, providing sweetness while keeping labeled sugar low. Glycerin is also a sugar alcohol and mildly sweet, but protein bars often use it as a humectant to keep the bar moist and soft. If you're like us and had no clue what humectant means, it's an ingredient that attracts and holds on to water or moisture. So an ingredient list doesn't necessarily tell us why an ingredient was added or which function matters most in the recipe, but its chemistry doesn't change based on intent.

We chose to use our best interpretation of FDA guidelines. The FDA's nutrition labeling rules treat glycerin differently from the sugar alcohols typically reported on Nutrition Facts labels. The regulations specifically address sugar alcohols such as sorbitol, mannitol, xylitol, maltitol, and erythritol. Glycerin is regulated separately, and the FDA recognizes it serves several functions. So for that reason, we're treating it differently too.

So what does that mean for glycerin on this No Sugar Alcohols page? Well, there are 61 brands we have listed on this page as not having sugar alcohols that have glycerin present. This includes several brands we think have very strong ingredient label quality. However, we understand if you have a different point of view and prefer to avoid glycerin. We've included a list of brands below that have glycerin used in all of their flavors and formulations.

What we found screening 1245 bars

26%
of bars contain a sugar alcohol
326 of 1245 bars contain at least one of the six sugar alcohols we screen for. Maltitol is the most common, ahead of every other sweetener on the list. It shows up across low-sugar and keto-marketed bars at every price point.
Almost no maltitol is a trace ingredient.
Just 4 of 202 bars containing maltitol list it inside a "contains 2% or less" clause, including FITCRUNCH Loaded Cookie, think! Oatmeal Chocolate Chunk. In the rest, including Anabar Fluff n' Butter, Barebells Fudge Brownie, it shows up in the first five ingredients, a real component of the recipe, not a rounding error.
35% of flagged bars show 0g sugar alcohol on the label anyway.
113 of the 326 bars that fail this screen list a sugar alcohol on the ingredient line but declare 0g (or leave it blank) on the Nutrition Facts panel, including Alani Munchies, Alani Rocky Road. The gram count on the label and the presence of the ingredient are two different things. We check the ingredient list, not just the number.
Barebells disqualifies almost entirely.
25 of 25 flavors fail the screen, mostly on maltitol or xylitol used to hit a low-sugar number on the label.
Whole-food bars dominate the qualifying pool.
KIND, Larabar, Bobo's, Aloha, GoMacro all qualify at or near 100%. Their sweetness comes from dates, honey, or fruit rather than a manufactured sugar alcohol.
A mixed lineup is common, not rare.
14 brands we checked split meaningfully between qualifying and disqualified flavors within the same lineup. Wonderslim is a clear case: 11 of 23 flavors qualify.
156 brands still represented.
Even with 26% of the database disqualified, the qualifying pool covers a wide range of protein levels, price points, and grades.
Maltitol is the single biggest driver.
It shows up in 202 bars, more than every other sugar alcohol on this screen combined with room to spare.

Frequently asked questions

We screen for Maltitol, Erythritol, Isomalto-oligosaccharides (IMO), Sorbitol, Xylitol, Isomalt. These are the sugar alcohols and sugar-alcohol-adjacent sweeteners that actually show up in protein bar ingredient lists, not a generic definition. Any bar listing one of these gets flagged, regardless of how small the amount looks on the label.
Maltitol, sorbitol, and xylitol are well known for causing gas, bloating, or a laxative effect in some people, especially at the multi-gram doses common in low-sugar protein bars. Erythritol is usually better tolerated at typical serving sizes, but individual sensitivity varies a lot. This guide screens for presence on the label, not tolerance, since that's the part we can measure.
Yes. Maltitol shows up in 202 of the 1245 bars we track (16%), more than any other sugar alcohol on our screen. Erythritol and Isomalto-oligosaccharides (IMO) are next, well behind.
Not technically. IMO is a prebiotic fiber syrup, not a true sugar alcohol, but it behaves the same way on a label and shows up in a lot of the same low-net-carb bars, so we screen for it alongside maltitol, erythritol, sorbitol, xylitol, and isomalt rather than giving it a pass.
Almost entirely. 25 of 25 Barebells flavors contain a sugar alcohol, most often maltitol or xylitol, part of how the brand hits its low-sugar numbers.
Usually, but only partially. The standard net-carb formula on this site is total carbohydrates minus fiber minus sugar alcohol, so a bar loaded with maltitol or erythritol can post a low net-carb number on the label while still containing a real amount of the ingredient itself. A low net-carb count doesn't mean a bar is sugar-alcohol-free.
Almost none of them, at least for maltitol. Only 1 of 200 bars containing maltitol list it inside a "contains 2% or less" clause. In bars like Anabar's Fluff n' Butter, Barebells's Fudge Brownie, it shows up in the first five ingredients, meaning it's a real component of the recipe, not a rounding error.
Yes, and it's common. Wonderslim splits close to the middle: 11 of 23 flavors qualify, usually because only some flavors lean on a low-sugar formula that needs a sugar alcohol to hit its numbers. Fluffy Nutter is the clean pick from that lineup.
919 bars across 156 brands clear our sugar alcohol screen, led by whole-food brands like KIND, Larabar, Bobo's that qualify 100% of the time. The full ranked list is in the table below, sorted by ingredient quality.
326 of the 1245 bars we track contain at least one sugar alcohol. Barebells disqualifies almost entirely, usually through maltitol or xylitol used to hit a low-sugar number on the label.
Sugar alcohols add sweetness and bulk with fewer usable calories and a smaller blood-sugar impact than regular sugar, which is why they show up so often in bars marketed as "low sugar" or "keto friendly." The tradeoff is digestive tolerance and, for some people, an artificial aftertaste.
Chemically, yes. But the FDA's own nutrition-labeling rule (21 CFR 101.9) doesn't include glycerin in the sugar alcohol list used for Nutrition Facts calculations the way it does maltitol, xylitol, sorbitol, erythritol, and isomalt. It's GRAS-listed separately as a food additive and shows up in bars mostly as a humectant that keeps the bar soft, not as the primary sweetener. We follow the FDA's own distinction here rather than guess at intent, so it doesn't count against a bar on this page. It appears in a meaningful share of the qualifying bars, so check the ingredient list yourself if you want to avoid it specifically.
Yes, and it's common. 113 of the 326 bars that fail this screen list a sugar alcohol on the ingredient line but show 0g, or leave the line blank, on the Nutrition Facts panel. That's part of why this guide is built by scanning the actual ingredient list for every bar rather than trusting the sugar alcohol gram count on the label.
